name: Asset Class
facts: Fixed income - limited risk to principal, interest paid periodically, capital returned at maturity; ~8-11% (2014).
Equity - no capital guarantee; Indian equities ~14-15% CAGR over 15 years; best companies >20% CAGR.
Real estate - rental income + capital appreciation; large outlay, illiquid, no official return metric.
Bullion (gold/silver) - ~8% CAGR over 20 years; via jewelry or ETFs.
Risk and return go hand in hand.
Fixed income can lose in real terms - a 9% FD with 10% inflation = -1% real return.
summary: A category of investment with particular risk and return characteristics - fixed income, equity, real estate, commodities (precious metals).

facts: Angel investors invest pre-revenue, take maximum risk (as much as promoter), small amounts.
Seed fund becomes initial share capital in the company's bank account.

Authorized shares - total shares available; issued shares are a subset allotted to holders.

Credible prior VC/PE rounds are a quality signal for IPO companies.

name: Initial Public Offering (IPO)
facts: Reasons - raise capex funds, spread promoter risk, exit for early investors, reward employees via ESOPs, visibility.
Sequence - appoint merchant banker -> registration statement to SEBI -> SEBI nod -> DRHP -> road show -> price band -> book building -> closure -> listing day.
DRHP contents - IPO size, shares offered, use of funds with timeline, business model, financials, MD&A, risks, management.
Book building - investors bid within the price band; listing price usually where max bids received.
Undersubscription signals negative sentiment; oversubscription Nx = bids/shares offered.
Green shoe option - over-allotment up to ~15% extra shares if oversubscribed.
Fixed price IPO has no band; cut-off price = final discovered price within band.
Most Indian IPOs follow book building.
caveats: Investors should read the DRHP; some companies list without healthy prior funding rounds.
summary: First offer of a company's shares to the public, moving it from private to listed (primary -> secondary market).
bot_use: Subscription multiple and anchor/VC pedigree are pre-listing sentiment features; listing day = start of secondary trading.

Caveats: - Investors should read the DRHP; some companies list without healthy prior funding rounds.
Bot Use: Subscription multiple and anchor/VC pedigree are pre-listing sentiment features; listing day = start of secondary trading.

name: Trader and Investor Types
facts: Day trader - opens and closes intraday, no overnight risk, ~5-6 stocks/day.
Scalper - very large size, very short hold, tiny per-share profit (e.g. 10,000 sh x Rs 0.10).
Swing trader - holds days to weeks.
Growth investor - companies growing on industry/macro trends.
Value investor - good companies beaten down by short-term sentiment (L&T 1200->690->1440).
Traders and investors differ on risk-taking ability and holding period.
summary: Traders (short view, unbiased long/short) vs investors (multi-year holding).

name: Bid, Ask and Market Depth
facts: Lowest ask has highest priority for sellers; highest bid for buyers (price priority).
A market buy of 10 shares with 2 @ best ask fills across several levels and moves LTP.
Understanding order stacking is critical for intraday traders.
summary: Bid = best prices buyers will pay; ask/offer = prices sellers demand; depth shows top 5 levels each side.
bot_use: Estimate slippage by walking the depth for order size; use bid/ask totals as order-flow imbalance feature.

Also: Bid price, Ask price, Offer, Order book depth, Spread
Bid = best prices buyers will pay; ask/offer = prices sellers demand; depth shows top 5 levels each side.
Formula: spread: best_ask - best_bid; mid: (best_ask + best_bid)/2
Facts: - Lowest ask has highest priority for sellers; highest bid for buyers (price priority). - A market buy of 10 shares with 2 @ best ask fills across several levels and moves LTP. - Understanding order stacking is critical for intraday traders.
Bot Use: Estimate slippage by walking the depth for order size; use bid/ask totals as order-flow imbalance feature.

name: Candlestick Trading Rules (3 assumptions)
facts: Marubozu is the only pattern exempt from the prior-trend rule.
Each pattern carries built-in entry and stop-loss; targets come from S&R.
Risk taker enters at ~3:20 PM on the pattern's last day after validating; risk averse enters next day near close only if that day confirms (blue for long, red for short).
The more days in a pattern, the better to enter on the pattern day itself (stars - enter on P3).
Long stop = lowest low of the pattern; short stop = highest high of the pattern.
Avoid trading candles with range < 1% (too subdued) or > 10% (stop too deep).
Once in a trade, do nothing until target or stop hits (trailing stops allowed).
summary: (1) Buy strength, sell weakness - buy on a blue day, sell on a red day; (2) be flexible but quantify and verify deviations; (3) look for a prior trend - bullish patterns need a prior downtrend, bearish need a prior uptrend.

name: Support and Resistance (S&R)
facts: Long trade target = nearest resistance; short trade target = nearest support.

Construction: (1) load 3-6 months (short-term, for intraday/BTST) or 12-18 months (long-term, for swing) of data; (2) find price action zones - hesitation after up move, hesitation after down move, sharp reversals; (3) find >= 3 zones at the same price, well spaced in time (e.g. >= 2 weeks apart); (4) fit a horizontal line.
More zones and wider time spacing = stronger level.
Treat S&R as a zone (e.g. 429 +/- 3), not a point.
Well-constructed S&R is usually respected but it is probabilistic.
Accumulation creates support; distribution creates resistance (Dow).

name: Moving Averages (SMA / EMA)
facts: Bullish when price > EMA; bearish when price < EMA.
Works brilliantly in trends, whipsaws in sideways markets.
Take all signals - many small losses, one big winner pays for them; can't pick the winner in advance.
summary: Rolling average of closes; SMA weights equally, EMA weights recent data more and reacts faster (preferred). Lagging trend-following tool.
text:
Moving Averages (SMA / EMA) (Indicator)
Also: SMA, EMA, Simple moving average, Exponential moving average, MA
Rolling average of closes; SMA weights equally, EMA weights recent data more and reacts faster (preferred). Lagging trend-following tool.
Formula: sma: mean(close[t-n+1..t]); ema: ema_t = alpha*close_t + (1-alpha)*ema_{t-1}, alpha = 2/(n+1)
Facts: - Bullish when price > EMA; bearish when price < EMA. - Works brilliantly in trends, whipsaws in sideways markets. - Take all signals - many small losses, one big winner pays for them; can't pick the winner in advance.

name: Dow Theory
facts: Indices discount everything.
Three trends - primary (1 to several years), secondary (counter-trend corrections, weeks to months), minor (daily noise).
All indices must confirm each other (Nifty, midcap, smallcap move together).
Volume must confirm - in uptrend volume rises on up moves, falls on dips; opposite in downtrend.
Sideways markets can substitute for secondary trends.
Close is the most sacred price.
Before going long on a pattern, check primary trend; trading against a secondary counter-trend needs caution.
summary: Charles Dow's framework (compiled by Hamilton) - 9 tenets on trends, confirmation and market phases.

name: Aroon and Aroon Oscillator
summary: Tushar Chande's time-since-high/low indicator (0-100); default 25 (Kite 14).
text:
Aroon and Aroon Oscillator (Indicator)
Tushar Chande's time-since-high/low indicator (0-100); default 25 (Kite 14).
Formula: aroon_up: 100*(n - periods_since_n_high)/n; aroon_down: 100*(n - periods_since_n_low)/n; oscillator: aroon_up - aroon_down
Conditions: buy: aroon_up > 50 and aroon_down < 30; sell: aroon_down > 50 and aroon_up < 30; strong_up: oscillator > 50; strong_down: oscillator < -50

name: Average True Range (ATR)

formula.atr: Wilder smoothing / average of TR over n

conditions.skip: if ATR-based stop violates RRR, skip trade

summary: Wilder's volatility measure including gaps; no direction; in price units.
bot_use: Volatility-normalised stops and position sizing.
text:
Average True Range (ATR) (Indicator)
Also: ATR, True range
Wilder's volatility measure including gaps; no direction; in price units.
Formula: true_range: max(high-low, abs(high-prev_close), abs(low-prev_close)); atr: Wilder smoothing / average of TR over n
Conditions: expected_range: price +/- ATR; volatility_stop_long: stop <= entry - ATR; volatility_stop_short: stop >= entry + ATR; skip: if ATR-based stop violates RRR, skip trade
Params: period: 14
Example: ATR 48 at 1320 -> range 1272-1368; long 1325 stop <= 1272.
Bot Use: Volatility-normalised stops and position sizing.

ATR Bands (Indicator)

name: Supertrend
facts: Fewer false signals than MA systems; works best in trending markets. Higher multiplier = fewer signals.

conditions.trail: hold long until close below green line

summary: ATR-based trailing trend line (Kite default period 7, multiplier 3); green below price in uptrends, red above in downtrends.
text:
Supertrend (Indicator)
ATR-based trailing trend line (Kite default period 7, multiplier 3); green below price in uptrends, red above in downtrends.
Formula: basic_upper: (high+low)/2 + mult*ATR; basic_lower: (high+low)/2 - mult*ATR
Conditions: buy: close crosses above supertrend (turns green); sell: close crosses below supertrend (turns red); trail: hold long until close below green line
Params: period: 7; multiplier: 3; suggested_multiplier: [3, 4]
Facts: - Fewer false signals than MA systems; works best in trending markets. Higher multiplier = fewer signals.

name: VWAP (Volume Weighted Average Price)
caveats: Intraday only; ignore jump at 9:15 open; lags price.
summary: Intraday cumulative volume-weighted typical price; gauges intraday direction and execution quality.
text:
VWAP (Volume Weighted Average Price) (Indicator)
Also: VWAP
Intraday cumulative volume-weighted typical price; gauges intraday direction and execution quality.
Formula: typical_price: (high + low + close)/3; vwap: cumsum(typical_price*volume)/cumsum(volume) (reset daily)
Conditions: intraday_bull: price > VWAP; intraday_bear: price < VWAP; good_long_fill: buy price < VWAP; good_short_fill: short price > VWAP
Caveats: - Intraday only; ignore jump at 9:15 open; lags price.

name: Compounding Effect
summary: Reinvesting gains lets money grow on itself; the longer you stay invested, the faster absolute wealth grows.
example: Rs 100 at 20% - took ~6 yrs to reach 300, next 300 in just 4 yrs; reinvesting gives 173 vs 160 when withdrawing profits after 3 yrs.
text:
Compounding Effect (Concept)
Reinvesting gains lets money grow on itself; the longer you stay invested, the faster absolute wealth grows.
Formula: future_value: P * (1 + r) ** n
Example: Rs 100 at 20% - took ~6 yrs to reach 300, next 300 in just 4 yrs; reinvesting gives 173 vs 160 when withdrawing profits after 3 yrs.

MD&A is the most important section - macro, industry, segment performance, outlook; compare with peers' ARs.
Check chairman's realism (e.g. claims 10% growth when history is 4-5% = red flag).
Standalone vs consolidated statements - prefer consolidated (includes subsidiaries).
Line items reference notes/schedules with details.
summary: Official yearly disclosure (data as of 31 March) - financial highlights, chairman's message, MD&A, 10-yr highlights, directors' report, corporate governance, financial statements, notice.

Annual Report (Concept)
Official yearly disclosure (data as of 31 March) - financial highlights, chairman's message, MD&A, 10-yr highlights, directors' report, corporate governance, financial statements, notice.
Facts: - Prefer AR over media websites (reclassification can distort). - MD&A is the most important section - macro, industry, segment performance, outlook; compare with peers' ARs. - Check chairman's realism (e.g. claims 10% growth when history is 4-5% = red flag). - Standalone vs consolidated statements - prefer consolidated (includes subsidiaries). - Line items reference notes/schedules with details.

name: Profit & Loss Statement (Income Statement)
facts: Other income (interest, dividends, royalty) should be small; large other income is a red flag.
Depreciation spreads tangible asset cost over useful life; amortisation for intangibles; P&L doesn't show the actual capex outflow (cash flow does).
Exceptional items are one-off.
Negative 'change in inventories' means more produced than sold.

formula.net_revenue_from_ops: sale of products (net of excise) + services + other operating revenue

summary: Revenue, expenses, tax and EPS for a period (year/quarter); top line = revenue, bottom line = PAT.
text:
Profit & Loss Statement (Income Statement) (Concept)
Also: P&L, Income statement
Revenue, expenses, tax and EPS for a period (year/quarter); top line = revenue, bottom line = PAT.
Formula: net_revenue_from_ops: sale of products (net of excise) + services + other operating revenue; total_revenue: revenue_from_operations + other_income; pbt: total_revenue - total_expenses - exceptional_items; pat: pbt - taxes; eps: pat / shares_outstanding
Facts: - Other income (interest, dividends, royalty) should be small; large other income is a red flag. - Depreciation spreads tangible asset cost over useful life; amortisation for intangibles; P&L doesn't show the actual capex outflow (cash flow does). - Exceptional items are one-off. - Negative 'change in inventories' means more produced than sold.

name: Balance Sheet
facts: Shareholders' funds appear on liability side because the company owes them to shareholders.
Reserves - capital, securities premium, general; surplus accumulates PAT, pays dividends.
Non-current liabilities (>12 months) - long-term borrowings, deferred tax liability (depreciation timing), long-term provisions (employee benefits).
Current liabilities - short-term borrowings (working capital), trade payables, other, short-term provisions.
Non-current assets - tangible/intangible fixed assets, CWIP, investments, long-term loans/advances.
Current assets - inventory, trade receivables, cash & equivalents, short-term loans/advances.
No debt is good but ask why (can't borrow? not expanding?).
P&L links - PAT -> surplus; credit sales -> receivables; purchases -> payables/inventory; capex -> depreciation; debt -> finance cost.
summary: Cumulative (flow-basis) statement of assets, liabilities and shareholders' equity; Assets = Liabilities + Equity.
text:
Balance Sheet (Concept)
Cumulative (flow-basis) statement of assets, liabilities and shareholders' equity; Assets = Liabilities + Equity.
Formula: equation: assets = shareholders_funds + non_current_liabilities + current_liabilities; equity: share_capital + reserves + surplus; share_capital: face_value * shares; shares_outstanding: share_capital / face_value; net_block: gross_block - accumulated_depreciation
Facts: - Shareholders' funds appear on liability side because the company owes them to shareholders. - Reserves - capital, securities premium, general; surplus accumulates PAT, pays dividends. - Non-current liabilities (>12 months) - long-term borrowings, deferred tax liability (depreciation timing), long-term provisions (employee benefits). - Current liabilities - short-term borrowings (working capital), trade payables, other, short-term provisions. - Non-current assets - tangible/intangible fixed assets, CWIP, investments, long-term loans/advances. - Current assets - inventory, trade receivables, cash & equivalents, short-term loans/advances. - No debt is good but ask why (can't borrow? not expanding?). - P&L links - PAT -> surplus; credit sales -> receivables; purchases -> payables/inventory; capex -> depreciation; debt -> finance cost.

name: Cash Flow Statement
facts: Revenue can include credit sales not yet collected - cash flow shows real liquidity.
Liabilities up -> cash up; assets up -> cash down.
Positive cash from operations is a sign of financial well-being; investors should focus on CFO.
Healthy investing outflow signals expansion.
summary: True cash generated/consumed across operating, investing and financing activities; net cash flow ties to balance sheet cash.
text:
Cash Flow Statement (Concept)
True cash generated/consumed across operating, investing and financing activities; net cash flow ties to balance sheet cash.
Formula: net_cash_flow: CFO + CFI + CFF
Facts: - Revenue can include credit sales not yet collected - cash flow shows real liquidity. - Liabilities up -> cash up; assets up -> cash down. - Positive cash from operations is a sign of financial well-being; investors should focus on CFO. - Healthy investing outflow signals expansion.

name: Financial Ratios (overview)
summary: Popularised by Benjamin Graham; categories - profitability, leverage, valuation, operating. A ratio alone is mute - compare with peers and its own trend; adjust for accounting policy changes; use averages of opening/closing balance sheet values.
text:
Financial Ratios (overview) (Concept)
Popularised by Benjamin Graham; categories - profitability, leverage, valuation, operating. A ratio alone is mute - compare with peers and its own trend; adjust for accounting policy changes; use averages of opening/closing balance sheet values.

name: EBITDA and EBITDA Margin
summary: Operating profitability excluding other income, finance cost and D&A; reflects management efficiency.
example: ARBL FY14 EBITDA 560 Cr on 3436 Cr = 16.3%; 4-yr EBITDA CAGR 21%.
text:
EBITDA and EBITDA Margin (Ratio)
Also: Operating profit margin
Operating profitability excluding other income, finance cost and D&A; reflects management efficiency.
Formula: ebitda: (total_revenue - other_income) - (total_expenses - finance_cost - depreciation); ebitda_margin: ebitda / (total_revenue - other_income)
Example: ARBL FY14 EBITDA 560 Cr on 3436 Cr = 16.3%; 4-yr EBITDA CAGR 21%.

name: PAT Margin (Net Profit Margin)
summary: Overall profitability after all expenses and tax.
text:
PAT Margin (Net Profit Margin) (Ratio)
Overall profitability after all expenses and tax.
Formula: pat_margin: pat / total_revenue
Example: ARBL 367/3482 = 10.5%.

name: Return on Equity (RoE)
caveats: Debt inflates RoE (pizza oven example 25% -> 31% -> 50% as debt rises); always inspect with DuPont and debt levels.
summary: Profit per unit of shareholders' equity; key investable attribute. Top Indian companies average 14-16%; author prefers >18-20% (checklist >25%) without high debt.
text:
Return on Equity (RoE) (Ratio)
Also: ROE
Profit per unit of shareholders' equity; key investable attribute. Top Indian companies average 14-16%; author prefers >18-20% (checklist >25%) without high debt.
Formula: roe: net_profit / avg_shareholders_equity
Caveats: - Debt inflates RoE (pizza oven example 25% -> 31% -> 50% as debt rises); always inspect with DuPont and debt levels.

name: DuPont Model
summary: RoE = Net profit margin x Asset turnover x Financial leverage; reveals quality of returns.
text:
DuPont Model (Formula)
RoE = Net profit margin x Asset turnover x Financial leverage; reveals quality of returns.
Formula: roe: (net_profit/net_sales) * (net_sales/avg_total_assets) * (avg_total_assets/avg_equity)
Example: ARBL 9.2% x 1.75 x 1.61 ~ 25.9%.

name: Return on Assets (RoA)
summary: Efficiency of asset use, adding back after-tax interest (tax shield) since lenders fund assets.
text:
Return on Assets (RoA) (Ratio)
Efficiency of asset use, adding back after-tax interest (tax shield) since lenders fund assets.
Formula: roa: (net_income + interest*(1 - tax_rate)) / avg_total_assets
Example: ARBL (367.4 + 4.76)/1955 = 19.03%.

name: Return on Capital Employed (ROCE)
summary: Return on total capital (debt + equity).
text:
Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) (Ratio)
Return on total capital (debt + equity).
Formula: roce: EBIT / (short_term_debt + long_term_debt + equity)
Example: ARBL 537.7/1446.2 = 37.18%.

name: Interest Coverage Ratio
summary: Ability to service interest from operating earnings; low coverage = default risk.
example: Jain Irrigation FY14 565.44/467.64 = 1.21x (weak).
text:
Interest Coverage Ratio (Ratio)
Ability to service interest from operating earnings; low coverage = default risk.
Formula: icr: EBIT / interest_expense; ebit: EBITDA - D&A
Example: Jain Irrigation FY14 565.44/467.64 = 1.21x (weak).

name: Debt to Equity Ratio
summary: Total (short + long-term) debt relative to equity; >1 indicates high leverage.
example: Jain Irrigation 3686.6/2175.5 = 1.69.
text:
Debt to Equity Ratio (Ratio)
Total (short + long-term) debt relative to equity; >1 indicates high leverage.
Formula: de: total_debt / total_equity
Conditions: caution: de > 1
Example: Jain Irrigation 3686.6/2175.5 = 1.69.

name: Debt to Asset Ratio
summary: Share of assets financed by debt.
example: Jain Irrigation ~45%.
text:
Debt to Asset Ratio (Ratio)
Share of assets financed by debt.
Formula: da: total_debt / total_assets
Example: Jain Irrigation ~45%.

name: Financial Leverage Ratio
summary: Assets supported per unit of equity; higher = more leveraged.
example: ARBL 1.61; Jain Irrigation 3.68.
text:
Financial Leverage Ratio (Ratio)
Assets supported per unit of equity; higher = more leveraged.
Formula: fl: avg_total_assets / avg_total_equity
Example: ARBL 1.61; Jain Irrigation 3.68.

name: Operating (Activity / Management) Ratios
caveats: High inventory turnover could reflect low production capacity - investigate funding
raw material access
scalability.

formula.cogs: materials + stock-in-trade purchases + stores & spares + power & fuel

summary: Efficiency of converting assets into revenue.
example: ARBL FAT 5.59, WCT 5.11, TAT 1.75, inventory turnover 7.8 (~47 days), receivables 8.24x (~44 days).
text:
Operating (Activity / Management) Ratios (Ratio)
Efficiency of converting assets into revenue.
Formula: fixed_asset_turnover: operating_revenue / avg_net_fixed_assets_incl_cwip; working_capital: current_assets - current_liabilities; working_capital_turnover: revenue / avg_working_capital; total_asset_turnover: operating_revenue / avg_total_assets; inventory_turnover: COGS / avg_inventory; inventory_days: 365 / inventory_turnover; receivable_turnover: revenue / avg_receivables; dso: 365 / receivable_turnover; cogs: materials + stock-in-trade purchases + stores & spares + power & fuel
Caveats: - High inventory turnover could reflect low production capacity - investigate funding - raw material access - scalability.
Example: ARBL FAT 5.59, WCT 5.11, TAT 1.75, inventory turnover 7.8 (~47 days), receivables 8.24x (~44 days).

name: Asset Turnover
summary: Revenue generated per rupee of average total assets.
text:
Asset Turnover (Ratio)
Revenue generated per rupee of average total assets.
Formula: asset_turnover: net_sales / avg_total_assets

name: Gross Profit Margin
summary: (Net sales - COGS)/Net sales; >20% suggests a moat.
text:
Gross Profit Margin (Ratio)
(Net sales - COGS)/Net sales; >20% suggests a moat.
Formula: gpm: (net_sales - cogs) / net_sales
Conditions: pass: gpm > 0.20

name: Earnings Per Share (EPS)
summary: PAT per outstanding share; EPS growth should track PAT growth (else dilution).
text:
Earnings Per Share (EPS) (Ratio)
PAT per outstanding share; EPS growth should track PAT growth (else dilution).
Formula: eps: pat / shares_outstanding

name: Price to Sales (P/S)
caveats: Higher-margin firms justify higher P/S - check profit margin.
summary: Price relative to sales per share; useful when earnings are cyclical or distorted.
text:
Price to Sales (P/S) (Ratio)
Price relative to sales per share; useful when earnings are cyclical or distorted.
Formula: ps: price / (total_revenue / shares)
Caveats: - Higher-margin firms justify higher P/S - check profit margin.
Example: ARBL 661/203.86 = 3.24x.

name: Price to Book Value (P/BV)
summary: Price relative to book (liquidation) value per share.
example: ARBL BV 79.8, P/BV 8.3x.
text:
Price to Book Value (P/BV) (Ratio)
Price relative to book (liquidation) value per share.
Formula: bvps: (share_capital + reserves - revaluation_reserves) / shares; pb: price / bvps
Example: ARBL BV 79.8, P/BV 8.3x.

name: Price to Earnings (P/E)
facts: Author avoids buying stocks above 25-30x earnings regardless of sector.
Earnings can be manipulated - watch frequent accounting policy changes, low depreciation provisions, earnings rising without cash flow and sales.
summary: Price paid per rupee of earnings - the 'financial ratio superstar'.
text:
Price to Earnings (P/E) (Ratio)
Also: PE
Price paid per rupee of earnings - the 'financial ratio superstar'.
Formula: pe: price / eps
Facts: - Author avoids buying stocks above 25-30x earnings regardless of sector. - Earnings can be manipulated - watch frequent accounting policy changes, low depreciation provisions, earnings rising without cash flow and sales.
Example: ARBL 661/21.49 = 30.76x.

name: Valuation Ratios
summary: Compare price with financial performance (P/S, P/BV, P/E); a mediocre business at a cheap valuation can beat an exciting one at a high valuation.
text:

facts: Key questions - what the company does, promoters' background, products, plants & capacity utilisation, raw material dependency (govt-regulated?), clients, competitors (monopoly/duopoly/oligopoly = higher margins), major shareholders, new products/geographies, revenue mix, regulation, bankers & auditors, labour issues, entry barriers, replicability in cheap-labour countries, number of subsidiaries.

name: Time Value of Money (FV, PV, NPV)
summary: Money's value changes over time due to opportunity cost; compounding moves money forward, discounting moves it back.
example: 5000 at 8.5% for 5 yrs = 7518.3; 10,000 in 6 yrs at 8.5% = 6129.5 today; pizza machine 5 lakh/yr x 10 yrs at 8.5% NPV = 32.8 lakh.
text:
Time Value of Money (FV, PV, NPV) (Formula)
Money's value changes over time due to opportunity cost; compounding moves money forward, discounting moves it back.
Formula: fv: amount * (1 + r) ** n; pv: amount / (1 + r) ** n; npv: sum(cf_t / (1 + r) ** t)
Example: 5000 at 8.5% for 5 yrs = 7518.3; 10,000 in 6 yrs at 8.5% = 6129.5 today; pizza machine 5 lakh/yr x 10 yrs at 8.5% NPV = 32.8 lakh.

Also: DCF, Intrinsic value
Intrinsic value = PV of projected FCF + PV of terminal value, adjusted for net debt, divided by shares.

Conditions: buy: price < lower band; hold: lower band <= price <= upper band (no fresh buy); overvalued: price > upper band (book profits or hold, never buy)

name: Mark to Market (M2M)
facts: Sum of daily M2M = total P&L. M2M plus margins virtually eliminate counterparty default.

formula.daily_m2m: (close_t - ref_price) * qty * direction, ref = entry on day 1 else close_{t-1}

summary: Daily settlement of futures P&L using previous close as reference; reference price resets to each day's close.
text:
Mark to Market (M2M) (Process)
Also: M2M, MTM
Daily settlement of futures P&L using previous close as reference; reference price resets to each day's close.
Formula: daily_m2m: (close_t - ref_price) * qty * direction, ref = entry on day 1 else close_{t-1}
Facts: - Sum of daily M2M = total P&L. M2M plus margins virtually eliminate counterparty default.
Example: Hindalco long 165, closes 168.3/172.4/171.6, exit 170.1 -> M2M +6600 +8200 -1600 -3000 = +10,200.

name: Impact Cost

bot_use: Slippage model in backtests; liquidity filter for universe.

Round-trip loss (buy at best ask, sell at best bid) as % of mid price; proxy for liquidity and market-order slippage.
Formula: impact_cost: (best_ask - best_bid) / ((best_ask + best_bid)/2)
Conditions: avoid_market_orders: impact_cost >> 0.0125%

name: Futures Pricing (Spot-Futures Parity)
facts: Market price differs slightly from fair value due to costs, taxes, margins, expected dividends; gap widens with days to expiry.
Futures > spot = premium (contango); futures < spot = discount (backwardation, from short-term demand/supply imbalance).
summary: Futures fair value = spot adjusted for risk-free carry minus dividends; basis (spread) = futures - spot; converges to zero at expiry.
text:
Futures Pricing (Spot-Futures Parity) (Formula)
Also: Fair value, Basis, Premium, Discount, Contango, Backwardation, Cost of carry
Futures fair value = spot adjusted for risk-free carry minus dividends; basis (spread) = futures - spot; converges to zero at expiry.
Formula: fair_value: spot * (1 + rf * days_to_expiry/365) - dividend; basis: futures - spot
Params: rf_proxy: RBI 91-day T-bill yield
Facts: - Market price differs slightly from fair value due to costs, taxes, margins, expected dividends; gap widens with days to expiry. - Futures > spot = premium (contango); futures < spot = discount (backwardation, from short-term demand/supply imbalance).
Example: Infosys spot 2280.5, rf 8.3528%, 7 days -> 2283 (market 2284); 34 days -> 2299; 80 days -> 2322.

name: European vs American Options
summary: European options exercise only at expiry based on expiry-day spot; American anytime before expiry (hence more expensive). All Indian options are European.
text:
European vs American Options (Concept)
European options exercise only at expiry based on expiry-day spot; American anytime before expiry (hence more expensive). All Indian options are European.

name: Call Option (long and short)
summary: Buyer bullish with limited risk (premium) and unlimited upside; seller expects price not to rise above strike, earns limited premium with unlimited risk and must post futures-like margin.
example: Bajaj Auto 2050 CE at 6.35 - breakeven 2056.35; at 2072 buyer +15.65, seller -15.65.
text:
Call Option (long and short) (Instrument)
Also: Long call, Short call, CE
Buyer bullish with limited risk (premium) and unlimited upside; seller expects price not to rise above strike, earns limited premium with unlimited risk and must post futures-like margin.
Formula: intrinsic_value_expiry: max(0, spot - strike); long_call_pnl: max(0, spot - strike) - premium_paid; short_call_pnl: premium_received - max(0, spot - strike); breakeven: strike + premium
Example: Bajaj Auto 2050 CE at 6.35 - breakeven 2056.35; at 2072 buyer +15.65, seller -15.65.

facts: Whether to buy a call or sell a put when bullish depends on premium attractiveness (pricing/IV).
summary: Buyer bearish - right to sell at strike; seller bullish/neutral, earns limited premium with large risk.
example: Bank Nifty 18400 PE at 315 - breakeven 18085; at 16510 buyer +1575.

Put Option (long and short) (Instrument)
Also: Long put, Short put, PE
Buyer bearish - right to sell at strike; seller bullish/neutral, earns limited premium with large risk.
Formula: intrinsic_value_expiry: max(0, strike - spot); long_put_pnl: max(0, strike - spot) - premium_paid; short_put_pnl: premium_received - max(0, strike - spot); breakeven: strike - premium

Example: Bank Nifty 18400 PE at 315 - breakeven 18085; at 16510 buyer +1575.

name: Four Option Positions Summary
facts: Buying to close a short (or selling to close a long) is a square-off, not a new long/short.
P&L formulas apply when held to expiry; premiums move continuously before expiry.
summary: Bullish - buy call or sell put; bearish - buy put or sell call. Buyers - limited risk, unlimited reward; sellers - limited reward, unlimited risk ('eat like a chicken, shit like an elephant' - Taleb/Das).
text:
Four Option Positions Summary (Rule)
Bullish - buy call or sell put; bearish - buy put or sell call. Buyers - limited risk, unlimited reward; sellers - limited reward, unlimited risk ('eat like a chicken, shit like an elephant' - Taleb/Das).
Facts: - Buying to close a short (or selling to close a long) is a square-off, not a new long/short. - P&L formulas apply when held to expiry; premiums move continuously before expiry.

name: Moneyness (ITM / ATM / OTM)
facts: Intrinsic value can never be negative (preserves limited-loss property).
summary: ITM has positive intrinsic value; ATM strike is nearest to spot; OTM has zero intrinsic value. Calls - strikes below ATM are ITM; puts - strikes above ATM are ITM. ITM premiums > OTM premiums.
text:
Moneyness (ITM / ATM / OTM) (Concept)
Also: ITM, ATM, OTM, In the money, Out of the money, At the money, Deep ITM, Deep OTM
ITM has positive intrinsic value; ATM strike is nearest to spot; OTM has zero intrinsic value. Calls - strikes below ATM are ITM; puts - strikes above ATM are ITM. ITM premiums > OTM premiums.
Conditions: call_itm: strike < spot; call_otm: strike > spot; put_itm: strike > spot; put_otm: strike < spot; atm: argmin |strike - spot|
Facts: - Intrinsic value can never be negative (preserves limited-loss property).

name: Option Greeks
summary: Sensitivities of premium - delta (spot), gamma (change in delta), theta (time), vega (volatility); computed by Black-Scholes; interact with each other.
text:
Option Greeks (Concept)
Sensitivities of premium - delta (spot), gamma (change in delta), theta (time), vega (volatility); computed by Black-Scholes; interact with each other.

name: Delta
facts: Delta changes with spot (moneyness changes).
Delta stages - predevelopment (deep OTM ~0, big % but needs huge move), take-off & acceleration (OTM->ATM, max bang for buck), stabilisation (ITM->deep ITM, delta -> 1).
Deep ITM option (delta 1) behaves like futures - can substitute with lower capital but watch liquidity.
Deltas are additive across options of same underlying; futures delta = 1; two ATM options ~ one future (but not a true surrogate - other Greeks act).
Short call = negative delta; short put = positive delta.
Delta ~ probability of expiring ITM (0.1 delta -> ~10%).
Delta-neutral positions (net delta 0, e.g. long ATM CE + long ATM PE) are insulated from direction but exposed to vol and time.
summary: Change in premium per 1-point change in underlying; calls 0..1, puts -1..0; ATM ~0.5, ITM -> 1, OTM -> 0. First derivative of premium.
bot_use: Size option positions by net delta exposure; use delta as ITM probability for strike selection; hedge to delta-neutral.
example: Nifty 8288, 8250 CE at 133, delta 0.55; Nifty to 8310 -> premium ~145.1.
text:
Delta (Greek)
Change in premium per 1-point change in underlying; calls 0..1, puts -1..0; ATM ~0.5, ITM -> 1, OTM -> 0. First derivative of premium.
Formula: premium_change: delta * underlying_change; position_delta: sum(qty_lots * delta * sign)
Facts: - Delta changes with spot (moneyness changes). - Delta stages - predevelopment (deep OTM ~0, big % but needs huge move), take-off & acceleration (OTM->ATM, max bang for buck), stabilisation (ITM->deep ITM, delta -> 1). - Deep ITM option (delta 1) behaves like futures - can substitute with lower capital but watch liquidity. - Deltas are additive across options of same underlying; futures delta = 1; two ATM options ~ one future (but not a true surrogate - other Greeks act). - Short call = negative delta; short put = positive delta. - Delta ~ probability of expiring ITM (0.1 delta -> ~10%). - Delta-neutral positions (net delta 0, e.g. long ATM CE + long ATM PE) are insulated from direction but exposed to vol and time.
Example: Nifty 8288, 8250 CE at 133, delta 0.55; Nifty to 8310 -> premium ~145.1.
Bot Use: Size option positions by net delta exposure; use delta as ITM probability for strike selection; hedge to delta-neutral.

name: Delta Neutral Position
summary: Combined options position with net delta ~0; unaffected by small directional moves, sensitive to volatility and time.
text:
Delta Neutral Position (Concept)
Combined options position with net delta ~0; unaffected by small directional moves, sensitive to volatility and time.

name: Gamma
facts: Gamma peaks at ATM; low for deep ITM/OTM.
Near expiry ATM gamma shoots up; ITM/OTM gamma -> 0.
Short gamma makes positions grow against you - a 10-lot short ATM (delta 5) can become delta 8.5 after a 70-pt adverse move.
Avoid shorting ATM/high-gamma options, especially near expiry; never short ATM/ITM hoping they expire worthless; OTM options are better short candidates if held to expiry.
summary: Rate of change of delta per point of underlying (2nd derivative of premium); always positive for long options. Long options = long gamma; short options = short gamma.
bot_use: Risk limits should use gamma-adjusted (scenario) delta, not lot counts.
example: 8400 CE delta 0.3 gamma 0.0025; +70 pts -> delta 0.475, premium 26 -> 47.
text:
Gamma (Greek)
Rate of change of delta per point of underlying (2nd derivative of premium); always positive for long options. Long options = long gamma; short options = short gamma.
Formula: new_delta: delta + gamma * underlying_change
Facts: - Gamma peaks at ATM; low for deep ITM/OTM. - Near expiry ATM gamma shoots up; ITM/OTM gamma -> 0. - Short gamma makes positions grow against you - a 10-lot short ATM (delta 5) can become delta 8.5 after a 70-pt adverse move. - Avoid shorting ATM/high-gamma options, especially near expiry; never short ATM/ITM hoping they expire worthless; OTM options are better short candidates if held to expiry.
Example: 8400 CE delta 0.3 gamma 0.0025; +70 pts -> delta 0.475, premium 26 -> 47.
Bot Use: Risk limits should use gamma-adjusted (scenario) delta, not lot counts.

name: Theta (Time Decay)
facts: Time decay is slow early in the series and accelerates sharply near expiry.
Selling early collects more time value but decays slowly; selling near expiry collects less but decays fast.
summary: Premium lost per day from passage of time, all else equal; options are depreciating assets. Long options = negative theta; short options = positive theta (friend of sellers).
example: Short at 54 with theta 0.75 -> ~51.75 after 3 days.
text:
Theta (Time Decay) (Greek)
Premium lost per day from passage of time, all else equal; options are depreciating assets. Long options = negative theta; short options = positive theta (friend of sellers).
Formula: premium_tomorrow: premium_today - theta
Facts: - Time decay is slow early in the series and accelerates sharply near expiry. - Selling early collects more time value but decays slowly; selling near expiry collects less but decays fast.
Example: Short at 54 with theta 0.75 -> ~51.75 after 3 days.

name: Premium = Intrinsic Value + Time Value
summary: Premium splits into intrinsic value (exercise value now) and time value (compensation to writer for time risk).
example: Nifty 8531, 8600 CE at 99.4 -> all time value; 8514.5, 8450 CE at 160 -> IV 64.5, TV 95.5.
text:
Premium = Intrinsic Value + Time Value (Formula)
Premium splits into intrinsic value (exercise value now) and time value (compensation to writer for time risk).
Formula: time_value: premium - intrinsic_value
Example: Nifty 8531, 8600 CE at 99.4 -> all time value; 8514.5, 8450 CE at 160 -> IV 64.5, TV 95.5.

name: Volatility (standard deviation of returns)
summary: Volatility = risk = standard deviation of (log) returns, expressed as %; higher SD = wider expected range.
example: Wipro daily vol 1.47% -> annual ~28% (NSE 1.34%/25.5%).
text:
Volatility (standard deviation of returns) (Concept)
Volatility = risk = standard deviation of (log) returns, expressed as %; higher SD = wider expected range.
Formula: log_return: ln(P_t / P_{t-1}); daily_vol: stdev(log_returns); annual_vol: daily_vol * sqrt(252 or 365); period_vol: daily_vol * sqrt(days); daily_from_annual: annual_vol / sqrt(365)
Example: Wipro daily vol 1.47% -> annual ~28% (NSE 1.34%/25.5%).

name: Standard Deviation and Variance
summary: Variance = mean of squared deviations from mean; SD = sqrt(variance); measures dispersion/consistency.
example: Billy SD 1.79 vs Mike SD 11.18 - Billy more consistent despite lower mean.
text:
Standard Deviation and Variance (Formula)
Variance = mean of squared deviations from mean; SD = sqrt(variance); measures dispersion/consistency.
Formula: variance: sum((x - mean)^2)/n; sd: sqrt(variance)
Example: Billy SD 1.79 vs Mike SD 11.18 - Billy more consistent despite lower mean.

name: Normal Distribution and Price Ranges
caveats: Real returns have fat tails - black swans happen more often than normal implies.
summary: Daily returns are a random walk but approximately normally distributed; ~68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD; outside 3 SD = black swan.
bot_use: Expected-move bands for strike selection, stop placement and position risk.
text:
Normal Distribution and Price Ranges (Concept)
Also: Bell curve, Random walk, Black swan
Daily returns are a random walk but approximately normally distributed; ~68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD; outside 3 SD = black swan.
Formula: period_mean: daily_mean * days; period_sd: daily_sd * sqrt(days); upper: spot * exp(period_mean + k*period_sd); lower: spot * exp(period_mean - k*period_sd)
Caveats: - Real returns have fat tails - black swans happen more often than normal implies.
Example: Nifty 8337, daily mean 0.04%, SD 1.046% -> 1-yr 1SD range 7777-10841; 30-day 1SD 7963-8930, 2SD 7520-9457.
Bot Use: Expected-move bands for strike selection, stop placement and position risk.

name: Vega
facts: 30 days to expiry, vol 15->30% moved premium ~95%; 15 days ~50%; 5 days ~47%.
Buy options when vol is expected to rise; sell when expected to fall.
High IV raises cost and lowers profit potential of debit spreads (bull call spread 72 cost at 20% IV vs 82 at 35%).
summary: Change in premium per 1% change in volatility; positive for long calls and puts; impact largest with more time to expiry and for OTM options.

Vega (Greek)
Change in premium per 1% change in volatility; positive for long calls and puts; impact largest with more time to expiry and for OTM options.
Facts: - 30 days to expiry, vol 15->30% moved premium ~95%; 15 days ~50%; 5 days ~47%. - Buy options when vol is expected to rise; sell when expected to fall. - High IV raises cost and lowers profit potential of debit spreads (bull call spread 72 cost at 20% IV vs 82 at 35%).

name: Black-Scholes Option Pricing
facts: Black & Scholes (1973)
Merton; Nobel 1997. Small model errors expected.

formula.call: S e^{-qT} N(d1) - K e^{-rT} N(d2)
formula.put: K e^{-rT} N(-d2) - S e^{-qT} N(-d1)

summary: Inputs - spot (or futures for futures-based options), strike, risk-free rate (RBI 91-day T-bill), implied volatility, dividend (if ex-date before expiry), calendar days to expiry; outputs theoretical call/put prices and Greeks.
text:
Black-Scholes Option Pricing (Model)
Also: BS model, Options calculator
Inputs - spot (or futures for futures-based options), strike, risk-free rate (RBI 91-day T-bill), implied volatility, dividend (if ex-date before expiry), calendar days to expiry; outputs theoretical call/put prices and Greeks.
Formula: d1: (ln(S/K) + (r - q + sigma^2/2) T) / (sigma sqrt(T)); d2: d1 - sigma sqrt(T); call: S e^{-qT} N(d1) - K e^{-rT} N(d2); put: K e^{-rT} N(-d2) - S e^{-qT} N(-d1)

Facts: - Moderate move quantified by volatility - volatile stocks 5-8%, less volatile stocks and indices < 5%. - Delta-neutral strategies react to volatility and time ('volatility based strategies'). - Winning on options can be addictive (reflexive vs reflective brain).

summary: Variance = dispersion of an asset's returns; covariance = co-movement sign of two assets; correlation = covariance / (sd_x sd_y). For k assets build the k x k variance-covariance matrix from the n x k excess-return matrix X, then the correlation matrix.

Formula: variance: sum((x - mean)^2)/N; covariance: sum((r1 - mean1)(r2 - mean2)) / (n - 1); cov_matrix: (1/n) * X^T X, X = returns - column means; corr_matrix: cov_matrix / (sd sd^T)
Facts: - Diagonal of covariance matrix = variances; correlation matrix diagonal = 1, symmetric. - Portfolio managers prefer low/negative covariance between holdings so they counterbalance.

name: Recovery Trauma (drawdown recovery math)

Position Sizing Techniques (Rule)
Decide how much capital/risk each trade gets. Methods - unit per fixed amount (e.g. 1 lot per 1L - simple, ignores risk, doesn't scale); percentage margin (fixed % of equity as margin per trade); percentage volatility (cap ATR-based volatility per position, e.g. 2% of equity); percentage risk (cap loss-at-stop at 1-3% of equity). Combine one equity model with one or two sizing methods.
Formula: pct_volatility_shares: (equity * vol_pct) / ATR; pct_risk_qty: (equity * risk_pct) / (abs(entry - stop) * lot_size)  [lots]; classic_5pct_rule: max exposure per trade = 5% of capital
Params: risk_per_trade_pct: [1, 3]; author_example_pct: 1.5; vol_pct: 2
Facts: - Professional traders rarely risk > 1-3% per trade. - Think about total portfolio volatility exposure (e.g. 15% of capital on a bad day - does it churn your stomach?).
Example: PEL ATR 76, equity 5L, 2% vol -> 10,000/76 = 131 shares; Tata Motors long 393.65 SL 390 lot 1500, 1.5% of 5L = 7,500 / 5,475 per lot -> 1 lot.
Bot Use: Mandatory sizing layer between signal and order - default to % risk with ATR/volatility stops, reduced-total-equity accounting.

name: Kelly Criterion (and capped Kelly)
caveats: Full Kelly is too aggressive - a 70% Kelly still leaves a large chance of a huge loss; estimates of W and R are noisy.
summary: Optimal bet fraction from win rate and win/loss ratio; author scales a capped risk budget by Kelly% rather than betting full Kelly.
bot_use: Scale per-trade risk by rolling backtest/live Kelly, capped.
example: W 0.6, avg win 4532, avg loss 3274 -> R 1.384 -> Kelly ~31%; with 5% cap -> risk ~1.55% of capital.
text:
Kelly Criterion (and capped Kelly) (Formula)
Optimal bet fraction from win rate and win/loss ratio; author scales a capped risk budget by Kelly% rather than betting full Kelly.
Formula: kelly_pct: W - (1 - W)/R; W: winning trades / total trades; R: average win / average loss; capped: risk_this_trade = kelly_pct * max_risk_pct (e.g. 5%)
Caveats: - Full Kelly is too aggressive - a 70% Kelly still leaves a large chance of a huge loss; estimates of W and R are noisy.
Example: W 0.6, avg win 4532, avg loss 3274 -> R 1.384 -> Kelly ~31%; with 5% cap -> risk ~1.55% of capital.
Bot Use: Scale per-trade risk by rolling backtest/live Kelly, capped.

summary: Track ratio = price_A / price_B; compute mean, SD (and SD table up to +/-3), and the cumulative normal 'density curve' value NORM.DIST(ratio, mean, sd, TRUE) daily; trade extremes, exit toward mean.

Pair Trading Method 1 - Ratio z-score / Density Curve (Mark Whistler) (Strategy)
Track ratio = price_A / price_B; compute mean, SD (and SD table up to +/-3), and the cumulative normal 'density curve' value NORM.DIST(ratio, mean, sd, TRUE) daily; trade extremes, exit toward mean.
Formula: ratio: price_A / price_B; density: Phi((ratio - mean)/sd)
Conditions: long_pair: density in ~[0.003, 0.025] (ratio at -2..-3 SD) -> buy A (numerator), sell B; short_pair: density in ~[0.975, 0.997] (+2..+3 SD) -> sell A, buy B; exit: ratio back inside 2 SD / toward mean (e.g. density ~0.16-0.84); density_map: 0.16=-1SD, 0.84=+1SD, 0.025=-2SD, 0.975=+2SD, 0.003=-3SD, 0.997=+3SD
Params: lookback: ~2 years daily (496 bars)

Treat the next-month minus current-month futures price difference as a mean-reverting series (prices already embed carry, dividends etc.); trade +/-1 SD deviations back to the mean.
Formula: spread: price_next_month - price_current_month; bands: mean +/- 1*sd (200-day continuous futures)
Conditions: sell_spread: spread > mean + 1sd -> sell next month, buy current month; buy_spread: spread < mean - 1sd -> buy next month, sell current month; exit: spread returns to mean

summary: Beta = relative risk vs benchmark (not inherent risk); alpha = risk-adjusted excess return; SD = inherent volatility; Sharpe = excess return per unit total volatility; Sortino = per unit downside deviation; capture ratios = share of benchmark up/down moves captured - prefer consistent low downside capture.

text:
Risk-Adjusted Performance Metrics (Beta, Alpha, SD, Sharpe, Sortino, Capture Ratios) (Formula)
Also: Sharpe ratio, Sortino ratio, Jensen alpha, Upside capture, Downside capture
Beta = relative risk vs benchmark (not inherent risk); alpha = risk-adjusted excess return; SD = inherent volatility; Sharpe = excess return per unit total volatility; Sortino = per unit downside deviation; capture ratios = share of benchmark up/down moves captured - prefer consistent low downside capture.
Formula: alpha: (R_fund - Rf) - beta * (R_bench - Rf); sharpe: (R - Rf) / sd; sortino: (R - Rf) / downside_deviation; upside_capture: fund_return_in_up_periods / bench_return_in_up_periods * 100; downside_capture: fund_return_in_down_periods / bench_return_in_down_periods * 100
Caveats: - Sharpe is meaningless for debt funds (ignores credit/rate risk).
Example: Fund 10%, bench 7%, Rf 4%, beta 0.75 -> alpha 3.75% (beta 1.3 -> 2.1%); Fund A (14%, sd 28%) and B (16%, sd 34%) both Sharpe 0.29 at Rf 6%.

facts: Steps - layout -> historical data (5 yrs, consolidated, from the annual report only) -> assumption sheet -> revenue model -> schedules (asset, debt, reserves) -> P&L/BS projections -> cash flow -> valuation.

name: Assumption Sheet - Ratio/Growth Drivers with Rolling Averages

formula.deferred_tax: deferred_tax = avg(deferred_tax / depreciation) * depreciation (more stable than growth)

summary: Express each line item historically as a ratio to a driver (BS items vs gross block; P&L items vs sales) or as a YoY growth rate; project with the rolling average of the last 4 years (Y6 = avg(Y2..Y5), Y7 = avg(Y3..Y6)) or an informed guess. Prefer drivers with a narrow, stable historical range.
text:
Assumption Sheet - Ratio/Growth Drivers with Rolling Averages (Process)
Express each line item historically as a ratio to a driver (BS items vs gross block; P&L items vs sales) or as a YoY growth rate; project with the rolling average of the last 4 years (Y6 = avg(Y2..Y5), Y7 = avg(Y3..Y6)) or an informed guess. Prefer drivers with a narrow, stable historical range.
Formula: ratio_driver: item_t / driver_t (e.g. liabilities / gross_block); growth_driver: item_t / item_{t-1} - 1; projection: item_{t+1} = rolling_mean(ratio, 4) * driver_{t+1}; deferred_tax: deferred_tax = avg(deferred_tax / depreciation) * depreciation (more stable than growth)

name: Inventory and Receivable Days
summary: Convert inventory (and receivables) from rupees to days, average the days, then convert back for projections; the days figures also reveal operating efficiency (fewer days = faster conversion to sales).
text:
Inventory and Receivable Days (Formula)
Convert inventory (and receivables) from rupees to days, average the days, then convert back for projections; the days figures also reveal operating efficiency (fewer days = faster conversion to sales).
Formula: inventory_days: avg(inventory_{t-1}, inventory_t) / materials_consumed_t * 365; receivable_days: avg(receivables_{t-1}, receivables_t) / sales_t * 365; back_to_value: inventory_t = inventory_days * materials_consumed_t / 365 (adjusting for averaging)

name: Revenue Sub-model
summary: Build revenue bottom-up from common-sense questions answered in the annual report - what they make, where they sell (domestic vs export), units x realisation per unit, capacity and utilisation. It also yields capacity utilisation, capex cycles and market share.
example: Bajaj Auto - motorcycles vs commercial vehicles, domestic vs export units; revenue ~Rs 29,111 Cr with exports ~Rs 12,216 Cr.
text:
Revenue Sub-model (Model)
Build revenue bottom-up from common-sense questions answered in the annual report - what they make, where they sell (domestic vs export), units x realisation per unit, capacity and utilisation. It also yields capacity utilisation, capex cycles and market share.
Formula: revenue: sum_segments(units_sold * avg_realisation); utilisation: units_produced / installed_capacity
Example: Bajaj Auto - motorcycles vs commercial vehicles, domestic vs export units; revenue ~Rs 29,111 Cr with exports ~Rs 12,216 Cr.

name: Base Rule (Roll-forward)
summary: Every schedule rolls forward - this year's closing balance is next year's opening balance; closing = opening + additions - deletions.
text:
Base Rule (Roll-forward) (Rule)
Every schedule rolls forward - this year's closing balance is next year's opening balance; closing = opening + additions - deletions.
Formula: closing: opening + additions - deductions; next_opening: closing_t

name: Asset Schedule (Gross Block, CAPEX, Depreciation, Net Block)
summary: Back out historical capex from changes in gross block; project capex from management guidance (best), historical averages, or a variable method; project depreciation with the proportion method (depreciation/gross block); roll accumulated depreciation forward; the net block flows back to the balance sheet and the depreciation to the P&L.
text:
Asset Schedule (Gross Block, CAPEX, Depreciation, Net Block) (Process)
Back out historical capex from changes in gross block; project capex from management guidance (best), historical averages, or a variable method; project depreciation with the proportion method (depreciation/gross block); roll accumulated depreciation forward; the net block flows back to the balance sheet and the depreciation to the P&L.
Formula: capex: gross_block_t - gross_block_{t-1} (+ disposals); depreciation_next: (dep_t / gross_block_t) * gross_block_{t+1}; accumulated_dep: acc_dep_{t-1} + dep_t; net_block: gross_block - accumulated_depreciation
Example: Dep 41.71 / GB 538.76 = 7.74%; projected GB 588.77 -> dep 45.58 Cr.

name: Debt Schedule
summary: Split debt into secured and unsecured using the notes, average the opening and closing balances to get the interest base, and project debt from management's capex/financing view; with no guidance, hold debt flat.
text:
Debt Schedule (Process)
Split debt into secured and unsecured using the notes, average the opening and closing balances to get the interest base, and project debt from management's capex/financing view; with no guidance, hold debt flat.
Formula: interest: avg(opening_debt, closing_debt) * interest_rate

name: Equity / Reserves Schedule
summary: Share capital (authorised >= issued >= subscribed/paid-up; shares = share capital / face value); reserves - securities premium (rises with fresh equity), general reserve, retained earnings (PAT flows in, dividends and DDT flow out). This is the main P&L-to-BS link.
text:
Equity / Reserves Schedule (Process)
Share capital (authorised >= issued >= subscribed/paid-up; shares = share capital / face value); reserves - securities premium (rises with fresh equity), general reserve, retained earnings (PAT flows in, dividends and DDT flow out). This is the main P&L-to-BS link.
Formula: shares_outstanding: paid_up_share_capital / face_value; retained_earnings: opening + PAT - dividends - transfers_to_general_reserve

name: Indirect Cash Flow and Balance Check
summary: Derive cash flow from P&L and balance-sheet changes - CFO (PAT + depreciation from the asset schedule +/- working-capital changes), CFI (capex, investments), CFF (debt, equity, dividends). Net cash flow plus opening cash gives closing cash, which plugs into the balance sheet; if the model is integrated correctly the balance sheet balances.
text:
Indirect Cash Flow and Balance Check (Process)
Derive cash flow from P&L and balance-sheet changes - CFO (PAT + depreciation from the asset schedule +/- working-capital changes), CFI (capex, investments), CFF (debt, equity, dividends). Net cash flow plus opening cash gives closing cash, which plugs into the balance sheet; if the model is integrated correctly the balance sheet balances.
Formula: closing_cash: opening_cash + CFO + CFI + CFF; check: total_assets - total_liabilities_and_equity == 0

name: Valuation Approaches (Relative, Option-based, Absolute)
summary: Relative - value like identical peers via multiples (fails if the sector is mispriced or the companies differ). Option-based - the firm's value depends on an event (e.g. R&D success), valued like an option (niche, tech). Absolute - intrinsic value from discounted cash flow (enterprise or equity). Decision - market price > fair price means overvalued, < means undervalued.
example: Peers at ~10x PAT -> a new peer with PAT 300 should trade ~Rs 3,000.
text:
Valuation Approaches (Relative, Option-based, Absolute) (Concept)
Relative - value like identical peers via multiples (fails if the sector is mispriced or the companies differ). Option-based - the firm's value depends on an event (e.g. R&D success), valued like an option (niche, tech). Absolute - intrinsic value from discounted cash flow (enterprise or equity). Decision - market price > fair price means overvalued, < means undervalued.
Conditions: overvalued: market_price > fair_price; undervalued: market_price < fair_price (buy only with margin_of_safety)
Example: Peers at ~10x PAT -> a new peer with PAT 300 should trade ~Rs 3,000.

name: Enterprise Value and Equity Value
summary: Rearranging the balance sheet - fixed assets = net debt + equity. Valuing the whole firm gives EV (discount FCFF at WACC); EV - debt + cash = equity value; divide by shares outstanding for fair value per share.
text:
Enterprise Value and Equity Value (Formula)
Rearranging the balance sheet - fixed assets = net debt + equity. Valuing the whole firm gives EV (discount FCFF at WACC); EV - debt + cash = equity value; divide by shares outstanding for fair value per share.
Formula: net_debt: debt - cash; equity_value: EV - debt + cash; fair_price: equity_value / shares_outstanding

name: Free Cash Flow to Firm (FCFF) and to Equity (FCFE)

formula.fcff_from_pat: PAT + D&A + interest*(1-tax) + deferred_tax - delta_working_capital - capex

summary: The firm is financed by debt and equity holders; FCFF is the cash available to both, and FCFE is what remains for equity after debt service. Discount FCFF at WACC and FCFE at the cost of equity.
text:
Free Cash Flow to Firm (FCFF) and to Equity (FCFE) (Formula)
The firm is financed by debt and equity holders; FCFF is the cash available to both, and FCFE is what remains for equity after debt service. Discount FCFF at WACC and FCFE at the cost of equity.
Formula: fcff_from_pat: PAT + D&A + interest*(1-tax) + deferred_tax - delta_working_capital - capex; fcff_from_ebit: EBIT*(1-tax) + D&A + deferred_tax - delta_working_capital - capex; fcfe: FCFF - interest*(1-tax) - principal_repayment + net_new_borrowing; working_capital: current_assets - current_liabilities

name: Interest Tax Shield / Effective Cost of Debt
summary: Interest is tax-deductible, so its after-tax cost is lower; add back interest*(1-t) in FCFF and use the after-tax cost of debt in WACC.
example: Interest 70 at 25% tax -> add back 52.5; kd 8% at 30% tax -> 5.6%.
text:
Interest Tax Shield / Effective Cost of Debt (Concept)
Interest is tax-deductible, so its after-tax cost is lower; add back interest*(1-t) in FCFF and use the after-tax cost of debt in WACC.
Formula: effective_cost_of_debt: kd * (1 - tax_rate)
Example: Interest 70 at 25% tax -> add back 52.5; kd 8% at 30% tax -> 5.6%.

name: CAPM - Cost of Equity
summary: The return equity holders expect is the risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium. Proxy Rf with the 10-year G-sec yield (CCIL/RBI); the long-term market return Rm is ~8-12%.
text:
CAPM - Cost of Equity (Formula)
The return equity holders expect is the risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium. Proxy Rf with the 10-year G-sec yield (CCIL/RBI); the long-term market return Rm is ~8-12%.
Formula: re: Rf + beta * (Rm - Rf); risk_premium: beta * (Rm - Rf)
Example: Rf 7.4586%, beta 1.3, Rm 8.5% -> Re 8.81%.

name: Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC)
summary: A blended discount rate for the whole firm; the cost of equity is always above WACC.
example: D 300, E 200, kd 8%, ke 12% -> 9.6% pre-tax; with a 30% tax shield -> 8.16%.
text:
Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) (Formula)
A blended discount rate for the whole firm; the cost of equity is always above WACC.
Formula: wacc: wd * kd*(1-t) + we * ke; wd: D/(D+E); we: E/(D+E)
Params: target_debt_to_equity: <= 50% (model default); tax_rate: 25% (model default)
Example: D 300, E 200, kd 8%, ke 12% -> 9.6% pre-tax; with a 30% tax shield -> 8.16%.

name: Terminal Value (Gordon Growth)
summary: Beyond the 5 explicit years, assume cash flows grow forever at roughly long-term inflation; DCF is extremely sensitive to this number, and it requires stable positive cash flows (DCF fails with negative ones).
text:
Terminal Value (Gordon Growth) (Formula)
Beyond the 5 explicit years, assume cash flows grow forever at roughly long-term inflation; DCF is extremely sensitive to this number, and it requires stable positive cash flows (DCF fails with negative ones).
Formula: tv: CF_final * (1 + g) / (r - g); pv_factor: 1 / (1 + r)^t; constraint: r > g; g ~ long-term inflation

name: DCF Implementation in the Model
summary: Inputs are Rf (10Y G-sec, ~7%), Rm (10-12%), beta, kd (~10%), tax (25%), target D/E (50%) and terminal g (~inflation). Steps - project FCFF Y6-Y10, compute TV at Y10, discount everything at WACC, sum to EV, subtract debt and add cash to get equity value, divide by shares for the fair price, then compare with the market price and run sensitivities on key assumptions.
bot_use: fair_value(inputs) -> upside = fair/price - 1; screen for upside > margin_of_safety; run grid sensitivity on g and WACC.
example: Year-3 FCFF 294.14 at WACC 10.25% -> PV 294.14/1.1025^3 = 219.49 Cr; Bajaj Auto fair value ~Rs 300 in the base case.

name: Insurance (Risk Transfer) - basics
facts: Order of priority - health insurance + term insurance -> emergency corpus -> goal investing.
Restrictions (waiting periods, co-pay, exclusions) exist to contain customer and hospital abuse.
summary: Insurance transfers the financial risk of rare, high-cost events to an insurer in exchange for a premium; health and term life insurance come before an emergency fund and before investing. name: Health Insurance (Indemnity)
facts: First 30 days - only accidental hospitalisation is covered.
Healthcare costs inflate ~6-7%/yr.
Premium increases are not caused by your own claims (urban myth).
summary: Pays hospitalisation bills up to the sum insured; the core protection product. Premiums rise every year (~4-6% medical inflation adjustment plus age-band jumps, occasionally regulator-approved repricing) but cannot be raised because you claimed.

name: Full Medical Disclosure (Non-disclosure risk)

conditions.rule: disclose all medical history, medication, smoking/alcohol on the form itself

summary: Declare every pre-existing condition and habit directly to the insurer on the proposal form - never rely on an agent's verbal assurance. Non-disclosure lets the insurer repudiate the claim or cancel the policy; a loading charge and a waiting period are far better than a rejected claim.

name: Perverse Incentives of Agents
summary: Agents earn commission on premium, so they upsell (Rs 50 lakh-1 crore covers via fear) or under-report your conditions to close the sale; evaluate advice by the adviser's incentive.

name: Choosing the Sum Insured
summary: Most expensive treatments rarely cross ~Rs 20 lakh; a Rs 10-20 lakh base cover (boosted by no-claim bonus and restoration) handles most cases. Rs 5 lakh may be inadequate within a decade given 6-7% medical inflation. A smaller cover is fine for the elderly or if you can't sustain the premium - lapsing a policy is the worst outcome. For rare huge bills, add a super top-up instead of buying a huge base cover.

name: Co-payment Clause

conditions.avoid_unless: mandatory, or buying for elderly with pre-existing diseases where it cuts premium sharply

summary: You pay a fixed % of every claim (e.g. 20%) in exchange for a lower premium - gives you 'skin in the game'. Usually a bad trade.
example: 20% co-pay saved Rs 1,800/yr on a Rs 7,000 premium, but a Rs 2 lakh claim cost Rs 40,000 out of pocket (~22 years of savings).

You pay a fixed % of every claim (e.g. 20%) in exchange for a lower premium - gives you 'skin in the game'. Usually a bad trade.

Example: 20% co-pay saved Rs 1,800/yr on a Rs 7,000 premium, but a Rs 2 lakh claim cost Rs 40,000 out of pocket (~22 years of savings).

name: Room Rent Cap / Proportionate Deduction

conditions.prefer: no room-rent cap; at least single private room allowed

summary: A cap on room rent (e.g. 1% of sum insured per day). Choosing a costlier room makes the insurer pay proportionately on all room-linked charges (surgeon, consultant, diagnostics), not only the rent difference.
example: Cap Rs 5,000, room Rs 10,000 -> insurer pays 50%; a Rs 50,000 surgeon fee pays only Rs 25,000.
text:

A cap on room rent (e.g. 1% of sum insured per day). Choosing a costlier room makes the insurer pay proportionately on all room-linked charges (surgeon, consultant, diagnostics), not only the rent difference.
Formula: payable_fraction: cap_rent / actual_rent; applied_to: room rent + associated charges
Conditions: prefer: no room-rent cap; at least single private room allowed
Example: Cap Rs 5,000, room Rs 10,000 -> insurer pays 50%; a Rs 50,000 surgeon fee pays only Rs 25,000.

name: Pre-existing Disease (PED) Waiting Period and Loading
summary: Declared conditions (diabetes, BP, etc.) trigger a PED waiting period (usually 2-4 years) during which related complications aren't covered, and/or a loading charge on the premium (typically 10-20%, up to ~150% for multiple illnesses); insurers may also reject the proposal.

Declared conditions (diabetes, BP, etc.) trigger a PED waiting period (usually 2-4 years) during which related complications aren't covered, and/or a loading charge on the premium (typically 10-20%, up to ~150% for multiple illnesses); insurers may also reject the proposal.
Params: ped_waiting_years: 2-4; loading: 10-20% typical, up to 150%

name: Waiting Periods (Initial, Specific Illness, PED)
summary: Three layers - initial 30 days (accidents only); specific-illness list (cataract, stones, deviated septum, hernia, joint replacement etc. - treatments that can be deferred), typically 2 years; PED waiting 2-4 years. Dengue, malaria, fractures, most cancers and heart conditions are covered after 30 days.

Dengue, malaria, fractures, most cancers and heart conditions are covered after 30 days.
Params: initial_days: 30; specific_illness_years: 2; ped_years: 2-4

name: Permanent Exclusions, Sub-limits, Non-medical Items, Blacklisted Hospitals

conditions.check_before_buying: no disease-wise sub-limits; read permanent exclusion list; check hospital blacklist; get a second opinion for expensive procedures

summary: Insurer defences against abuse - permanent exclusions (substance/alcohol-induced illness, cosmetic treatment, external congenital conditions); disease-wise sub-limits (e.g. cardiac Rs 2.5L, knee Rs 2.75L, cataract Rs 50k regardless of cover) - avoid policies with them; non-medical consumables excluded; only 'just and reasonable' treatment per medical council norms paid; blacklisted hospitals can be refused.
example: Rs 10 lakh cover, slipped-disc bill Rs 4.36 lakh, insurer paid only Rs 2 lakh due to a sub-limit.

name: Family Floater Policy
summary: One shared sum insured for self, spouse and children at a discount to individual plans; risks within a family are correlated, so the shared cover can run out. Children must exit after an age limit; parents usually excluded. Online discounts are small (<5% first year); real discounts come from wellness programmes, multi-year tenure or floaters.

name: Group and Employer Health Insurance

conditions.rule: employer cover + personal base policy (or a super top-up aligned to the employer cover)

summary: Customised contracts for a group via a master policyholder (bank, employer). Cheaper and often with no waiting periods (invaluable for those with serious PEDs), but pricing is repriced yearly at the insurer's discretion, features are set by the master policyholder, and cover ends if you leave the job or the group dissolves (re-underwriting then). Keep a personal policy alongside an employer cover.

name: Restoration Benefit
summary: Restores the sum insured after a claim. Useful in floaters; often neutered by fine print (only for a different illness, or only after the cover is fully exhausted). Verdict - not a gimmick, but buyer beware.

name: No Claim Bonus (NCB)
summary: Cover grows (e.g. +50% of base) for each claim-free year up to a cap (50%-200% depending on plan); some plans claw it back after a claim, never below base. Verdict - not a gimmick.
example: Rs 10L base, 50% NCB -> 15L after 1 claim-free year, 20L after 2; a claim drops it back to 15L.

name: Health Insurance Features - Gimmick or Not
facts: Network hospitals (cashless) - not a gimmick.
AYUSH cover - slightly gimmicky (only in government-certified AYUSH hospitals with inpatient admission).
Restoration benefit - not a gimmick, but buyer beware.
Pre/post hospitalisation (e.g. 30/60 days to 60/180 days) - near-universal, nothing extraordinary.
Day care (<24h procedures like chemo, dialysis, appendicitis) - not a gimmick; make sure it's covered.

Claim settlement ratio - not a gimmick, but needs context (with ICR).
Porting - not a gimmick.

name: Top-up Health Plan
summary: Large cover above a deductible, but the deductible applies to each hospitalisation separately, so several mid-size bills below the deductible are never paid. Verdict - highly gimmicky.
text:

Large cover above a deductible, but the deductible applies to each hospitalisation separately, so several mid-size bills below the deductible are never paid. Verdict - highly gimmicky.

name: Super Top-up Health Plan

formula.payout: max(0, sum(claims_in_policy_year) - deductible), capped at cover

conditions.dates: super top-up renewal aligned with base/employer policy year

summary: Very cheap large cover (e.g. Rs 50 lakh for ~Rs 1,000s/yr) that pays once the aggregate bills within a policy year cross the deductible. Choose the deductible equal to the existing base or employer cover, and align policy-year dates with that cover, otherwise the deductible must be met again in a new term.
example: Deductible Rs 5L, bills 7L then 3L in the same year -> super top-up pays 2L + 3L; a plain top-up pays 2L + 0.

Very cheap large cover (e.g. Rs 50 lakh for ~Rs 1,000s/yr) that pays once the aggregate bills within a policy year cross the deductible. Choose the deductible equal to the existing base or employer cover, and align policy-year dates with that cover, otherwise the deductible must be met again in a new term.
Formula: payout: max(0, sum(claims_in_policy_year) - deductible), capped at cover
Conditions: deductible: = base/employer cover; dates: super top-up renewal aligned with base/employer policy year
Example: Deductible Rs 5L, bills 7L then 3L in the same year -> super top-up pays 2L + 3L; a plain top-up pays 2L + 0.

name: Claim Settlement Ratio (CSR) and Incurred Claims Ratio (ICR)

conditions.icr_high: >100% -> insurer losing money (regulator may force merger)
conditions.icr_low: ~50% -> may be stingy on large claims

summary: CSR = % of claims settled; it can be gamed (clearing last year's backlog, settling many small claims while rejecting large ones, combining motor/health for general insurers). Read it alongside ICR and scale (large customer base). Get the numbers from the IRDAI annual report.
text:
Claim Settlement Ratio (CSR) and Incurred Claims Ratio (ICR) (Ratio)
CSR = % of claims settled; it can be gamed (clearing last year's backlog, settling many small claims while rejecting large ones, combining motor/health for general insurers). Read it alongside ICR and scale (large customer base). Get the numbers from the IRDAI annual report.
Formula: csr: claims_settled / (claims_booked + outstanding_start - outstanding_end); icr: claims_paid / net_premiums_collected
Conditions: icr_high: >100% -> insurer losing money (regulator may force merger); icr_low: ~50% -> may be stingy on large claims

name: Porting a Health Policy
summary: Move a policy to a new insurer while carrying over waiting-period credit. Apply 45-60 days before renewal and prove continuous coverage with documents; credit applies only up to the old sum insured (plus bonus) - extra cover serves fresh waiting periods; the new insurer may re-underwrite. Verdict - not a gimmick; usually better than buying fresh.

Apply 45-60 days before renewal and prove continuous coverage with documents; credit applies only up to the old sum insured (plus bonus) - extra cover serves fresh waiting periods; the new insurer may re-underwrite. Verdict - not a gimmick; usually better than buying fresh.

name: Stop Loss
summary: A pre-defined exit price that caps the loss on a trade; placed at a technical level (recent low/high, pattern low) or volatility-based (ATR/SD multiple) and never widened once placed.
text:
Stop Loss (Rule)
A pre-defined exit price that caps the loss on a trade; placed at a technical level (recent low/high, pattern low) or volatility-based (ATR/SD multiple) and never widened once placed.

name: Dividend Yield
